q: What is continuous batching and why is it central to LLM serving throughput?
a: Traditional static batching groups requests and processes them together, but because each request generates a different number of output tokens, the whole batch waits for the longest one, leaving the GPU idle for finished sequences. Continuous batching, also called in-flight batching, schedules at the level of individual decoding steps. After every step, finished sequences are removed from the batch and newly arrived requests are inserted immediately, so the GPU stays busy and short requests are not held back by long ones. Combined with efficient memory management for the KV cache, it can raise throughput several times over naive serving and cut queueing latency. Engines like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM and Text Generation Inference implement it. As an operator, the relevant knobs are maximum batch size, maximum number of batched tokens and scheduling policy, which trade throughput against per-request latency, and I tune them with load tests that mimic my real prompt and output lengths.
f: What knob trades latency for throughput?
Why does static batching waste GPU time?
p: Continuous batching adds and removes sequences at every decoding step, so the GPU never waits for the longest request. It multiplies throughput and cuts queueing. Tune batch limits with realistic load tests.
tip: Say you tune it with a load test that matches real lengths.

q: What is PagedAttention and how does vLLM manage GPU memory?
a: The KV cache for each request grows as tokens are generated and its final length is unknown in advance. Allocating one contiguous block sized for the maximum length wastes huge amounts of memory through fragmentation and over-reservation, limiting how many requests fit. PagedAttention borrows the idea of virtual memory paging: the KV cache is divided into fixed-size blocks, allocated on demand and mapped through a block table, so a sequence's cache need not be contiguous and waste is minimal. Blocks can also be shared between requests that have the same prefix, for example parallel sampling or a common system prompt, with copy-on-write. The result is much higher batch sizes on the same GPU and therefore higher throughput. vLLM reserves a fraction of GPU memory for this cache, controlled by gpu-memory-utilization, and exposes cache usage as a metric that I watch to avoid preemption.
f: What happens when the KV cache is full?
How does prefix sharing work?
p: PagedAttention stores the KV cache in fixed-size on-demand blocks mapped by a block table, eliminating fragmentation and enabling prefix sharing. That fits more concurrent requests per GPU. Watch cache usage and preemptions.
tip: Compare it to virtual memory paging to make it memorable.

q: How do you choose between vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Text Generation Inference and llama.cpp?
a: I choose by hardware, model coverage, performance needs and operational fit. vLLM is a flexible, widely adopted engine with broad model support, an OpenAI-compatible API, continuous batching, PagedAttention, quantisation and multi-LoRA, and is a strong default on NVIDIA and increasingly on other accelerators. TensorRT-LLM from NVIDIA compiles models for maximum performance on NVIDIA GPUs, which can win on latency and throughput, at the cost of a build step and tighter hardware coupling. Text Generation Inference from Hugging Face is a mature server with good integration into that ecosystem. llama.cpp targets CPUs and modest hardware, including laptops and edge devices, using GGUF quantised models, which is ideal for local and low-cost deployments, but not for high-concurrency serving. I benchmark candidates with my own model and traffic profile, check API compatibility and metrics, and weigh the upgrade and support burden.
f: What does OpenAI-compatible API buy you?
When is llama.cpp the right answer?
p: vLLM is the flexible default, TensorRT-LLM maximises NVIDIA performance with a build step, TGI fits the Hugging Face ecosystem, llama.cpp suits CPU and edge. Benchmark on your own model and traffic.
tip: End with: I would benchmark on my workload.

q: How do you scale an LLM inference service on Kubernetes, and why is CPU-based autoscaling a poor fit?
a: Standard HPA on CPU or memory does not reflect load on a GPU-bound inference server, because the CPU may be idle while the GPU queue is saturated. I scale on signals that track demand: number of waiting or running requests, queue depth, KV cache utilisation, time to first token or tokens per second, exposed by the server as Prometheus metrics and fed to HPA through the custom metrics API, or to KEDA. Scaling out is slow because a new replica must schedule onto a GPU node, pull a large container image, and load tens or hundreds of gigabytes of weights, which can take minutes. So I keep warm capacity, use image and model caching on nodes, preload weights from fast storage, scale up early with conservative scale-down, and sometimes use predictive scaling. Cluster autoscaler or Karpenter provisions GPU nodes, and I set pod disruption budgets and graceful draining of in-flight requests.
f: Why is scale-up slow for LLM pods?
Which metric would you scale on?
p: Scale on queue depth, running requests, KV cache use or time to first token via custom metrics or KEDA, not CPU. Cold starts are slow because of GPU nodes, image pulls and weight loading, so keep warm capacity and cache models.
tip: Mention the multi-minute cold start as the design constraint.

q: How do you reduce model load time and cold start for large models?
a: Cold start has three parts: scheduling a GPU node, pulling the container image, and loading weights into GPU memory. I attack each. Keep a buffer of ready nodes or use fast provisioning so scheduling is quick. Keep images small, split the model out of the image, and pre-pull images to nodes with a DaemonSet or an image cache. Store weights on fast storage close to the GPU, such as local NVMe, a node-level cache populated once, or a high-throughput shared file system or object store with parallel readers, rather than downloading from the internet on every start. Use safetensors format and loaders that stream or memory-map weights, and tensor parallel loading across GPUs in parallel. Quantised weights are smaller and load faster. Finally, avoid frequent scale to zero for latency-sensitive services and use readiness probes that only pass after the model is fully loaded and warmed up.
f: Why a readiness probe after warm-up?
What is the benefit of safetensors?
p: Pre-provision GPU nodes, keep images small and pre-pulled, cache weights on local NVMe or fast shared storage in safetensors format, use quantised weights, avoid scale to zero for latency-sensitive services, and gate readiness on warm-up.
tip: Break cold start into node, image and weights.

q: What metrics do you monitor for an LLM inference service?
a: I split them into user-facing, capacity and quality signals. User-facing: time to first token, inter-token latency, end-to-end latency percentiles, request success and error rates, and tokens per second. Capacity: requests running and waiting, queue time, batch size, KV cache utilisation, preemptions, GPU utilisation, memory use, memory bandwidth, temperature, power and errors such as ECC and XID from the driver, collected by DCGM exporter. Cost and usage: input and output tokens per tenant, model and route, cache hit rate for prompt caching, and cost per request. Quality and safety: guardrail triggers, refusal rate, format validation failures, user feedback and evaluation scores on sampled traffic. I set SLOs on time to first token and success rate, alert on queue growth and cache saturation before users feel it, and break dashboards down by model, version and tenant, so a regression is easy to localise.
f: Which metric would you alert on first?
Why track tokens per tenant?
p: Track time to first token, inter-token latency, error rate and throughput; running and waiting requests, KV cache use, GPU health through DCGM; tokens and cost per tenant; and quality signals. Set SLOs and alert on queue growth.
tip: Say you alert on queue growth, a leading indicator.

q: How do you serve many tenants or models efficiently on shared GPUs?
a: I choose the isolation level by requirements. For many fine-tuned variants of the same base model, multi-LoRA serving loads one base model and swaps small adapters per request, which is the most efficient option. For multiple different models, I either dedicate pools per model, which is simple but can leave capacity idle, or use a multi-model server that loads and unloads models on demand, accepting load latency. GPU sharing methods include time slicing, which has no memory isolation, MPS for concurrent kernels, and MIG on supported GPUs, which partitions the hardware with strong isolation. A routing layer or LLM gateway applies authentication, per-tenant rate limits and quotas, model selection, and priorities so that one tenant cannot starve others. I add per-tenant metrics for chargeback, and I keep sensitive tenants on dedicated GPUs if the data policy demands it.
f: Time slicing versus MIG?
How do you prevent noisy neighbours?
p: Use multi-LoRA for variants of one base model, pools or on-demand loading for different models, and GPU sharing through MPS or MIG. A gateway enforces per-tenant limits, priorities and metering; dedicate GPUs where policy demands.
tip: Name MIG for hard isolation and multi-LoRA for efficiency.

q: What is an LLM gateway and what does it provide?
a: An LLM gateway is a proxy that sits between applications and one or more model providers or self-hosted servers, presenting a unified API, often OpenAI compatible. It centralises concerns that every team would otherwise reimplement. Routing and fallback: choose a model by task, cost or availability, and fail over to another provider when one is down or rate limited. Authentication and authorisation: issue virtual keys per team or application, with model access policies. Rate limits, quotas and budgets per key, plus usage metering and cost attribution. Caching of identical or semantically similar requests, retries and timeouts. Guardrails such as PII redaction and content filtering, and logging, tracing and audit. It also lets me change models without touching applications. The risks are being a single point of failure and an added latency hop, so it needs high availability, horizontal scaling and careful handling of logged prompts, which may contain sensitive data.
f: What are the risks of logging prompts at the gateway?
How does fallback routing work?
p: A gateway provides one API in front of many models with routing and fallback, virtual keys and policies, quotas and cost metering, caching, guardrails and tracing. It needs HA and careful prompt logging.
tip: Say it makes model changes invisible to application teams.

q: How do you roll out a new model version safely?
a: I treat a model like any other release, with extra attention to behaviour changes that unit tests do not catch. First, offline evaluation: run the candidate on the evaluation set and compare quality, safety, format validity, latency and cost with the current model, with a clear go or no-go threshold. Second, shadow deployment, where real traffic is copied to the candidate and responses are compared but not shown to users. Third, a canary release to a small percentage of traffic or a few tenants, with monitoring of quality proxies, errors, latency, cost and user feedback, and automatic rollback criteria. Then a gradual ramp, keeping the previous version deployed and warm for quick rollback. Model, prompt and configuration are versioned together, and I pin versions explicitly. After release, I keep sampling outputs for review, because subtle quality regressions appear only on real traffic.
f: What is shadow traffic?
What would trigger an automatic rollback?
p: Offline evaluation with thresholds, shadow traffic comparison, canary with quality, cost and latency monitoring and automatic rollback criteria, then gradual ramp while keeping the old version warm. Version model, prompt and config together.
cmds: kubectl argo rollouts set image llm-api model=registry/model:v2
tip: Shadow traffic catches regressions without exposing users.

q: What is speculative decoding and when does it help?
a: Autoregressive decoding is slow because each token needs a full pass through a large model, and the GPU is underused during that memory-bound step. Speculative decoding uses a small, fast draft model, or a draft head, to guess several next tokens quickly, then the large target model verifies all of them in a single parallel pass, accepting the longest correct prefix and discarding the rest. Because the target model's verification determines the final output, the result is identical in distribution to normal decoding, while the speed can improve by roughly two to three times when the draft model's guesses are often accepted. It helps most for latency-sensitive, low-batch workloads and predictable text like code. It helps less at high batch sizes, where the GPU is already saturated, and it uses extra memory for the draft model. I benchmark the acceptance rate, since that determines the gain.
f: Does speculative decoding change the output quality?
What determines the speed-up?
p: A small draft model proposes tokens and the large model verifies them in one pass, giving the same output distribution with up to two to three times lower latency when acceptance is high. Best for low-batch, latency-sensitive loads.
tip: Say acceptance rate decides the benefit.

q: How do you implement streaming responses and handle timeouts and retries for LLM APIs?
a: LLM responses can take many seconds, so I stream them using server-sent events or WebSockets, sending tokens as they are generated, which greatly improves perceived latency. The stack between client and model must support streaming: proxies and load balancers need buffering disabled and idle timeouts raised, because default timeouts, for instance 60 seconds, kill long generations. I set separate timeouts for connection, time to first token and total duration, and cancel upstream generation when the client disconnects, which saves GPU time. Retries need care: retry only on safe, transient failures such as 429, 503 and network errors, with exponential backoff and jitter and a retry budget, and never blindly retry after partial output without idempotency, since the user may already have seen text. Rate limit responses should honour the retry-after header. I also apply backpressure and queue limits, so overload fails fast instead of growing latency.
f: Why cancel generation on client disconnect?
Which errors are safe to retry?
p: Stream with SSE, disable proxy buffering and raise idle timeouts, set separate connect, first-token and total timeouts, cancel on disconnect, and retry only transient errors with backoff, jitter and budgets.
tip: Say disconnect cancellation saves GPU time.

q: How do you run LLM inference at the edge or on CPUs, and what are the limits?
a: For privacy, offline use, or low cost, small quantised models can run on CPUs, laptops, phones or edge boxes. The usual stack is a runtime such as llama.cpp or ONNX Runtime with models in a compact quantised format like GGUF at four or five bits, which fits a few-billion-parameter model into a few gigabytes of RAM. Performance depends on memory bandwidth more than core count, so unified-memory systems and fast RAM help, and CPU instruction sets such as AVX2, AVX-512 or ARM NEON matter. Expect much lower throughput than GPUs, a few to a few tens of tokens per second for small models, and limited concurrency, so it suits single-user or low-volume workloads, local assistants, and on-device features rather than a high-traffic service. Model quality is limited by size, so I choose narrow tasks, test accuracy on the target hardware, and handle updates and model distribution securely.
f: Why does memory bandwidth dominate?
How do you distribute models to edge devices?
p: Run small quantised models with llama.cpp or ONNX Runtime on CPUs or edge devices. Throughput is bandwidth-limited and concurrency low, so use it for private, offline or low-volume narrow tasks and validate accuracy on the target hardware.
tip: Position it for privacy and offline, not for high concurrency.

q: How do you design disaster recovery and high availability for an LLM service?
a: I plan at several layers. Compute: run multiple replicas across availability zones, with pod anti-affinity and spare GPU capacity, since losing one GPU node should not exceed the SLO. Model artifacts: store weights in durable, versioned storage replicated to another region, so a recovery site can start without depending on an external download that may be unavailable. Dependencies: the vector database, caches, gateway and secrets need their own HA and backups. Failure of the model itself: a fallback path, to a smaller local model, a second provider, or a degraded mode with cached or retrieval-only answers, which keeps the product useful. Traffic management with health checks that test real generation, circuit breakers and load shedding that protects the system under overload. Finally I set RTO and RPO targets, test failover regularly with game days, and track GPU capacity in the secondary region, because GPUs are scarce and may not be available on demand during an outage.
f: Why is GPU capacity a DR risk?
What is a degraded mode for an LLM product?
p: Multi-AZ replicas with spare GPU capacity, replicated versioned model artifacts, HA for vector DB and gateway, fallback models or degraded modes, health checks that test generation, load shedding, and tested failover. Reserve DR GPU capacity.
tip: Mention that GPUs may not be available on demand in a disaster.

q: How do you schedule GPU workloads on Kubernetes? Explain device plugins and resource requests.
a: GPUs are exposed to Kubernetes through the device plugin framework. The NVIDIA device plugin, usually installed with the GPU Operator, runs on each GPU node, advertises the extended resource nvidia.com/gpu to the kubelet, and handles allocation. A pod requests GPUs in its resource limits, for example nvidia.com/gpu: 1, and the scheduler places it on a node with enough free GPUs. GPUs are integer resources and cannot be overcommitted or fractionally requested by default. The container runtime, configured with the NVIDIA container toolkit, mounts the driver libraries and device files into the container. To control placement I label and taint GPU nodes, so only GPU workloads land there, and use node selectors or affinity to choose a GPU type. Newer Kubernetes features such as dynamic resource allocation provide richer device selection. For efficiency, I consider MIG or time slicing for small workloads.
f: Why taint GPU nodes?
What does the container toolkit do?
p: The device plugin advertises nvidia.com/gpu, pods request it in limits, and the NVIDIA container toolkit injects drivers. Taint and label GPU nodes, and use MIG or time slicing to share small workloads.
cmds: kubectl describe node gpu-1 | grep nvidia.com/gpu
tip: Say GPUs are integer resources by default.

q: What does the NVIDIA GPU Operator install and why use it?
a: The GPU Operator automates everything a Kubernetes node needs to use NVIDIA GPUs, as a set of managed components deployed through a custom resource. It installs and manages the GPU driver, the container toolkit, the device plugin, DCGM and the DCGM exporter for metrics, node feature discovery and GPU feature discovery that label nodes with GPU model and capabilities, and optionally MIG manager and the Kubernetes validator. Without it, you would bake drivers into node images and manage versions and upgrades by hand, which is error prone across many nodes. The operator makes upgrades declarative, keeps components consistent, and supports driver containers that match the kernel. Considerations are compatibility between driver, CUDA and Kubernetes versions, ensuring the operator's pods tolerate GPU node taints, and in managed clouds, where the provider may supply drivers, deciding whether to use the operator or the provider's integration.
f: What does GPU feature discovery label?
When would you skip the operator?
p: The Operator deploys drivers, container toolkit, device plugin, DCGM exporter, feature discovery and MIG manager declaratively, keeping versions consistent. Check driver and CUDA compatibility and cloud-provider driver options.
cmds: kubectl get node gpu-1 -o json | jq '.metadata.labels | with_entries(select(.key|test("nvidia")))'
tip: List the components to show you know what it manages.

q: Explain MIG, time slicing and MPS for sharing a GPU. When would you use each?
a: Multi-Instance GPU, available on some data-centre GPUs, partitions one physical GPU into several isolated instances, each with dedicated compute slices, memory and bandwidth, giving predictable performance and hard isolation, which is good for multi-tenant inference and small jobs. Partitions are fixed profiles, so changing them needs reconfiguration. Time slicing lets several pods share one GPU by taking turns, configured through the device plugin; it works on any GPU and is simple, but there is no memory isolation, so one pod can exhaust memory, and latency is variable. Multi-Process Service allows kernels from several processes to run concurrently on the GPU, improving utilisation for many small workloads, with optional resource limits but weaker fault isolation than MIG. I use MIG when isolation and predictability matter, time slicing for dev and test where cost matters most, and MPS to raise utilisation for cooperating workloads.
f: Which approach gives memory isolation?
What are MIG's constraints?
p: MIG gives hard-partitioned isolated instances with predictable performance, time slicing is simple but has no memory isolation, and MPS runs kernels concurrently for better utilisation. Pick by isolation and predictability needs.
cmds: kubectl get cm time-slicing-config -n gpu-operator -o yaml
tip: Match each method to its isolation guarantee.

q: How do you monitor GPU health and utilisation, and what do the signals mean?
a: I use the DCGM exporter, which publishes GPU metrics to Prometheus. Utilisation shows how busy the compute engines are, but it only says a kernel was running, not how efficiently, so I also watch memory used and memory copy utilisation, SM activity and tensor core activity, which show real work. Memory use against capacity predicts out-of-memory errors. Temperature, clock throttling reasons and power draw reveal cooling or power limits that reduce performance. Error signals matter most for reliability: ECC errors, XID errors in the kernel log, which indicate faults such as a fallen-off-the-bus GPU, and NVLink errors. A GPU with growing correctable errors or recurring XID events should be drained and repaired. I also correlate GPU metrics with application metrics, since low GPU utilisation with high queue time suggests a CPU or data-loading bottleneck, whereas high utilisation with growing latency means capacity is exhausted.
f: Why is utilisation misleading?
What is an XID error?
p: Use DCGM exporter for utilisation, memory, SM and tensor activity, temperature, throttling, power and ECC and XID errors. Drain GPUs with repeated errors, and correlate with queue and latency metrics.
tip: Say GPU utilisation alone is a weak efficiency signal.

q: What is tensor, pipeline and data parallelism, and how do they affect inference deployment?
a: These are ways to spread work across GPUs. Data parallelism runs a full copy of the model on each GPU and splits the requests, which scales throughput when the model fits on one GPU. Tensor parallelism splits each layer's matrices across GPUs, so every GPU computes part of every layer, which lets a model too big for one GPU run and cuts latency, but it needs very fast interconnect such as NVLink, because the GPUs exchange data at every layer. Pipeline parallelism splits the model by layers into stages on different GPUs, passing activations along, which needs less bandwidth and suits multi-node setups but introduces pipeline bubbles. For inference I use tensor parallelism within a node over NVLink, pipeline parallelism across nodes if needed, and data parallelism replicas for scale. I also check topology with nvidia-smi, because a poor PCIe layout can hurt tensor parallel performance badly.
f: Why does tensor parallelism need NVLink?
How do you choose the tensor parallel size?
p: Data parallelism replicates the model to scale throughput, tensor parallelism splits layers across GPUs to fit big models and cut latency but needs NVLink, pipeline parallelism splits by layers across nodes. Check topology.
tip: Say tensor parallel stays inside a node on NVLink.

q: How do you size GPU memory and capacity for serving a given model?
a: I start with arithmetic. Weight memory is the number of parameters times bytes per parameter: a seven-billion parameter model needs about 14 GB at 16-bit, 7 GB at 8-bit and about 4 GB at 4-bit. On top of that comes the KV cache, which depends on layers, hidden dimension, number of KV heads, sequence length and concurrent sequences, plus activation and framework overhead, so I leave 10 to 20 percent headroom. For a target concurrency and context length I compute the cache requirement and check it fits, then choose GPU memory and tensor parallelism accordingly. Throughput planning uses a benchmark with realistic prompts: measure tokens per second per GPU at my latency SLO, then divide the expected peak tokens per second by that number and add spare capacity for failures and growth. I validate with load tests, because theory and real engines can differ.
f: How do you estimate KV cache size?
What headroom do you reserve?
p: Weights are parameters times bytes per parameter, add KV cache for concurrency and context, plus 10 to 20 percent overhead. Then benchmark tokens per second per GPU at the SLO and size for peak plus failure headroom.
tip: Show the arithmetic: parameters times bytes, plus cache, plus headroom.

q: How do you handle GPU node failures and drain them safely in Kubernetes?
a: GPU nodes fail in ways CPU nodes rarely do: driver crashes, ECC or XID errors, GPUs falling off the bus and overheating. I detect them with DCGM health checks, node problem detector and alerts on error counters, and I automate marking affected nodes unschedulable. To drain, I cordon the node, then evict pods with the eviction API so that pod disruption budgets are respected, giving inference servers time to finish in-flight requests through a pre-stop hook and a termination grace period long enough for streaming generations. For training jobs, I rely on checkpoints, so that the job resumes from the latest one on another node, and on a controller or framework that restarts failed workers, such as an elastic launcher. After draining, I run diagnostics, reset or replace the GPU, and return the node with a validation test. Spare capacity and node auto-repair reduce the impact.
f: Why a long termination grace period?
How do checkpoints limit the cost of failure?
p: Detect with DCGM and error alerts, cordon and drain respecting PDBs, let inference drain in-flight streams with pre-stop hooks, resume training from checkpoints, then diagnose, repair and validate before returning the node.
cmds: kubectl cordon gpu-3 && kubectl drain gpu-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
tip: Mention checkpoints for training and drain time for inference.

q: What networking matters for multi-node GPU training and inference?
a: Distributed training and large-model inference exchange large tensors between GPUs constantly, so the interconnect is as important as the GPUs. Within a node, NVLink and NVSwitch provide very high bandwidth between GPUs, far beyond PCIe. Across nodes, I need a high-bandwidth, low-latency fabric, usually InfiniBand or RoCE Ethernet at 200 to 800 gigabits per node, with RDMA, and GPUDirect RDMA so network cards read GPU memory directly without CPU copies. Collective libraries such as NCCL implement all-reduce and related operations, and tuning involves topology awareness, correct network interface selection, and avoiding oversubscribed switches. In Kubernetes, this means multiple network interfaces through Multus or the SR-IOV device plugin, host networking or RDMA device plugins, and careful pod placement within the same rack or spine for locality. Common problems are NCCL picking the wrong interface, packet loss on RoCE without proper congestion control, and straggler nodes slowing everyone.
f: What does GPUDirect RDMA avoid?
How do you diagnose slow all-reduce?
p: Use NVLink within a node and InfiniBand or RoCE with RDMA and GPUDirect across nodes, NCCL tuned for topology, multiple interfaces in Kubernetes, and locality-aware placement. Watch for wrong interfaces, RoCE loss and stragglers.
tip: Say the interconnect often limits scaling more than the GPUs.

q: How would you build a shared GPU platform for several teams? Consider quotas, queues and fairness.
a: I treat GPUs as a scarce shared resource with a proper scheduling layer. Teams get namespaces with resource quotas on GPU counts, plus priority classes so that production inference can preempt batch jobs. For batch and training, a queueing system such as Kueue, Volcano or a similar scheduler provides gang scheduling, so a multi-GPU job starts only when all its GPUs are available, and fair-share or borrowing between teams, so idle quota is used and returned when needed. Interactive notebooks get time limits and idle culling. Node pools are separated by GPU type with labels and taints, and users request by class rather than model name. Cost visibility through per-team usage reports and showback encourages efficient use. I add utilisation dashboards, since low-utilisation allocations are the usual waste, and policy on maximum job duration, with checkpointing encouraged, to keep the system fair and efficient.
f: What is gang scheduling?
How does borrowing work between queues?
p: Namespaces with GPU quotas, priority classes, a queueing layer such as Kueue or Volcano with gang scheduling and fair-share borrowing, node pools by GPU type, notebook culling and showback. Dashboards expose idle allocations.
tip: Name gang scheduling and fair-share borrowing.

q: How do you improve low GPU utilisation in a training or inference workload?
a: I find the bottleneck before changing anything. Profile with the framework profiler, Nsight or DCGM metrics to see whether the GPU is waiting. Common causes: slow data loading, where CPU preprocessing or storage throughput starves the GPU, fixed with more workers, caching, faster storage, prefetching and storing data in efficient formats. Small batch sizes that do not fill the device, fixed by larger batches or continuous batching for inference. Python overhead and synchronisation points, reduced with compiled graphs, fused kernels and avoiding unnecessary host to device copies. Communication overhead in multi-GPU jobs, addressed by overlapping communication and compute, and improving the network. Uneven work between ranks, causing stragglers. Mixed precision such as bf16 improves speed and memory. I change one thing at a time and measure samples or tokens per second, not just the utilisation percentage, since efficiency is what ultimately matters.
f: How do you tell data loading from compute bottlenecks?
Why is utilisation percentage not enough?
p: Profile first. Typical fixes: faster data pipelines and caching, larger batches or continuous batching, fewer host-device syncs, overlap communication with compute, mixed precision, and balanced ranks. Measure throughput, not utilisation alone.
tip: Say you measure tokens or samples per second.

q: What are the options for getting GPU capacity, and how do you handle scarcity?
a: Options include on-demand cloud GPUs, which are flexible but may be unavailable and costly; reserved or committed capacity, cheaper but locked in; spot or preemptible instances, much cheaper but interruptible, good for fault-tolerant batch work; specialised GPU cloud providers; and owning on-premises hardware, with the best unit economics at high steady utilisation but long lead times and operational burden. Because supply can be constrained, I plan capacity ahead, use a mix: a reserved baseline for production inference, spot for training with checkpoints, and on-demand burst for peaks. I reduce demand by quantisation, smaller models, batching and caching, and by routing easy requests to cheaper models. Multi-region or multi-provider flexibility helps availability, as does portable infrastructure code. I track utilisation and queue times, and review quotas with the provider early, since quota increases can take days.
f: Which workloads suit spot GPUs?
How do you decide between buying and renting?
p: Mix reserved capacity for production inference, spot with checkpointing for training, and on-demand for bursts; consider specialised providers or owned hardware at high steady use. Cut demand with quantisation, smaller models and routing.
tip: Say quotas and lead times are part of capacity planning.
